newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Postpone Bosnia local poll to 1997 - OSCE monitor.
newsitem.headline: Postpone Bosnia local poll to 1997 - OSCE monitor.

text.p: Bosnian municipal elections scheduled for November should be postponed until next spring to ensure proper voting conditions, the OSCE's independent election monitor said on Tuesday.

"The date of these elections should be dependent on the fulfilment of the basic technical and political criteria and conditions...laid out in the Dayton agreement," said Ed van Thijn, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's coordinator for international monitoring.
"A good preparation cannot and should not happen overnight. The necessary conditions cannot be met in this calendar year."
Asked when the election should be held, van Thijn said it would take at least four months to satisfy the minimal conditions set forth in the 1995 Dayton peace agreement.
He observed that since elections during Bosnia's harsh winter were impractical, the earliest likely date would be April 1997.
The OSCE was charged under Dayton with staging Bosnia's first post-war national elections, held on September 14th.
Municipal polls, originally scheduled to be part of that vote, were postponed when it became clear there had been widespread irregularities in registering voters.
The OSCE's head of mission in Bosnia, Robert Frowick, recently indicated that the municipal elections would be rescheduled for late November.

But van Thijn, who operates independently from Frowick, said all 25 of his long-term field monitors had reported "that the situation on the ground does not allow for municipal elections to be held in November".
He said voter registration problems needed to be resolved, and refugees would require greater security assurances before being able to cross ethnic borders to vote.
Hundreds of thousands of refugees and displaced persons driven from their homes during the 43-month war have the right under Dayton to return to their former places of residence to vote or live.
Few have taken that opportunity for fear of reprisals from rival ethnic groups.

Nationalist Moslem, Serb and Croat parties who dominated the September vote for federal and regional assemblies are keen to demonstrate clear political control over their respective territories by registering wins in the local elections, whenever they are held.

Moslems, the largest losers of territory as a result of war-time ethnic cleansing, aim to get their voters back into pivotal areas like Srebrenica, Doboj and Brcko -- a move that would be fiercely opposed by Serbs who control those towns.
Van Thijn, speaking to reporters in Sarajevo, reiterated previous reservations about the September 14 elections and pointedly refused to describe them as "free and fair".

But the OSCE monitor said his team had not unearthed any evidence of widespread fraud and insisted that despite problems in the vote-counting process there was no sign of imperfections of a magnitude sufficient to affect the overall outcome.
The OSCE had to recount a large portion of the vote after finding major errors by locally-staffed counting houses, but this confirmed the original results putting nationalist parties in power.
